title: Monotone circuits versus monotone span programs
formal:
Do there exist nonconstant monotone Boolean functions \(f_n:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}\), one for each \(n\ge1\), with polynomial-size monotone circuits but without polynomial-size monotone span programs over \(\mathbb F_2\)? More precisely, does some family satisfy
\[\exists C,d\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge1,\quad\mathrm{mC}(f_n)\le C(n+1)^d,\]
\[\forall C',d'\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n_0\ge1\ \exists n\ge n_0,\quad\mathrm{mSP}_{\mathbb F_2}(f_n)>C'(n+1)^{d'}?\]
Yes. Published lower bounds from STOC 2018 give such a separation even when the monotone span programs may use any field. This record is archived as resolved.
why: The separation establishes that short monotone logical computations need not admit short monotone linear-algebraic representations. It also identifies a limitation of linear secret-sharing representations, whose size is linked to monotone span programs.
status_note: Resolved affirmatively by Pitassi and Robere, STOC 2018, DOI 10.1145/3188745.3188914. The original chapter explicitly works over GF(2). The published proceedings §2.1 and §7 (Theorems 7.1–7.2 with applications) and the full ECCC TR17-165 §4.2 and Appendix B were read to verify the model, row-size measure, total layered-connectivity witness and arbitrary-field lower bounds. Polynomial monotone circuits versus quasipolynomial monotone span programs already meet the target; the stronger generation separation is additional. Source theorem parameters are polynomially related to input-bit length. This is a source-verified published resolution, not a new proof or a claimed Lean formalization of the full result.

sentences: The historical question asks whether polynomial-size monotone circuits can coexist with superpolynomial monotone span-program size.
The source works over GF(2) and measures span-program size by the number of rows.
STOC 2018 proves quasipolynomial monotone span-program lower bounds for layered directed connectivity over every field.
The same functions have polynomial-size monotone circuits, giving the required affirmative separation.
The card is resolved and archived, with the stronger generation-function separation recorded as additional context.

definitions:
A Boolean function is monotone if \(x_i\le y_i\) for every coordinate implies \(f(x)\le f(y)\). Nonconstant monotone functions have \(f(0^n)=0\) and \(f(1^n)=1\); the known separating families satisfy these conditions, so constant-function conventions play no role. A monotone circuit is a finite acyclic circuit with input variables, binary AND and OR gates, and unrestricted reuse of intermediate outputs. It contains no negated input or NOT gate. Its size is the number of gates; \(\mathrm{mC}(f)\) is the minimum size of a circuit computing \(f\) exactly on every input. Circuits for different input lengths may be chosen independently: this is a nonuniform size question, without a requirement for an algorithm generating the circuits.

The field \(\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}\) has addition and multiplication modulo 2. A monotone span program over this field consists of a finite matrix \(M\in\mathbb F_2^{s\times t}\), a fixed nonzero target vector \(w\in\mathbb F_2^t\), and a label \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) on each row; labels may repeat. On input \(x\), keep exactly those rows whose labels \(i\) satisfy \(x_i=1\). Accept if and only if some linear combination of the kept rows equals \(w\). The size is \(s\), the number of rows, and \(\mathrm{mSP}_{\mathbb F_2}(f)\) is the smallest row count of an exact program for \(f\). Allow any finite column dimension and any fixed nonzero target; an invertible change of coordinates gives the equivalent all-ones target convention used in the source. No restriction on coefficients, sparsity or row-label multiplicity is imposed beyond belonging to \(\mathbb F_2\). The program is chosen separately for each input length and has no randomness or error.

Counting rows is the source’s algebraic size measure, not a running time for Gaussian elimination or a count of matrix bits. Redundant dimensions can be removed: all rows and the target lie in a subspace of dimension at most \(s+1\). The lower bound still quantifies over all finite-dimensional representations. A positive literal enables a vector, but the linear combinations may cancel, so the algebra itself is not restricted to a monotone semiring.

Polynomial size means one fixed polynomial bound for the whole family, not a separately selected exponent at each length. The second displayed condition says that no fixed polynomial bounds the minimum span-program sizes; it supplies violations at arbitrarily large lengths. Both comparisons use the number \(n\) of input bits. A graph-parameterized family with polynomially related input length can be placed at its corresponding lengths and extended to other lengths, so a change between graph size and full input length must be accounted for. The field is fixed to \(\mathbb F_2\) as in the opening of the source chapter; the later theorem is stronger because its lower bound holds over every field.
answer_criterion: The original benchmark asks for a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the two displayed size conditions for one family. A positive answer must specify the family, establish monotonicity, give polynomial-size monotone circuits and prove the superpolynomial lower bound against every monotone span program over \(\mathbb F_2\). A refutation would exclude all such families. Exact asymptotic size bounds are required; numerical tolerance is not relevant. The mathematical existence question has a published affirmative answer and is therefore retired from the open benchmark. Its archival resolution records the published theorem; this review does not claim that a complete Lean formalization has been supplied.

context_blocks.text: Span programs combine two kinds of behavior: adding input-enabled rows is monotone, but linear algebra permits cancellation. They can therefore be much smaller than monotone AND/OR circuits for some functions. The source asks whether the reverse efficiency gap also exists.

The 2016 work obtained the reverse separation over the real field. That result alone would not answer the chapter’s GF(2) question: linear dependence can change when the characteristic of the field changes.

The 2018 theorem gives \(N^{\Omega(\log N)}\) monotone span-program lower bounds over every field for suitable layered directed-connectivity functions with \(N\) edge-input bits. These functions have polynomial-size monotone circuits. The bound exceeds every fixed polynomial and directly resolves the requested separation over \(\mathbb F_2\).

In the layered-connectivity witness, the possible directed edges go only between consecutive layers, and the input selects which edges are present. The output asks whether the designated first-layer source can reach the last-layer target. This is a total monotone function of the edge bits, not a promise on which graphs are given.

The same paper obtains a stronger, weakly exponential separation using a generation problem. Those stronger bounds are additional progress, not needed to satisfy the source’s superpolynomial threshold.

This settles the historical comparison without proving general Boolean circuit lower bounds or showing that linear algebra is always weaker. The significance is an incomparability of two monotone representation models on different explicit families.
